extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics, mathematicians, and mathematics educators
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating or summarizing a scholarly book (Lakatos's Proofs and Refutations) about the methodology of mathematical discovery, proof, and pedagogy, with emphasis on conjecture/refutation, counterexamples, and presentation style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjecture-and-refutation methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical inquiry begins with a conjecture and, by way of tentative proof (a thought-experiment), decomposes the conjecture into subconjectures; counter-instances provoke re-examination, identification of a 'guilty' subconjecture, and substitution by a tighter subconjecture, after which the process repeats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review quotes Lakatos's account as the central logical pattern of scientific/mathematical discovery: begin with conjecture, use tentative proofs to expose subconjectures, use counterexamples to convict and replace faulty subconjectures, and iterate. This cyclical process is presented as a preferable heuristic to simple formal vindication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of counterexamples to expose hidden assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Counter-instances (examples that violate the conjecture) are used to reveal which assumptions or subconjectures in a proof are guilty and need revision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review discusses several counterexamples (e.g., a hollow solid 'cube within a cube', two tetrahedra sharing only an edge/vertex, a polyhedron with a square tunnel, Kepler's star polyhedron) as illustrations of how counterexamples force re-examination of proofs and prompt explicit stipulations that exclude such cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative refinement and careful sequencing of restrictions (successive amputations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Refinements of a conjecture should be performed in successive, ordered 'amputations' so as not to disqualify too many counterinstances at once and so as to preserve illustrative examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review praises Lakatos's ordering of successive restrictions to keep pedagogical examples available; it warns that premature or large-scale restrictions early in treatment would remove useful illustrations and that excessive prolonging of curtailments can at times feel strained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical use of case studies and varied examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Use multiple, varied case studies to illustrate the dialectic of conjecture and refutation and to open new fields of inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The volume's supplements (e.g., Leibniz/Cauchy continuity example) show that presenting different historical/mathematical case studies helps teach methodological values and demonstrates how the conjecture/refutation process generalizes across problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Layered presentation: dialogue plus scholarly footnotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Present material on two levels: a lively dialogue (teacher and pupils) for the heuristic, pedagogical demonstration, and extensive footnotes that supply historical precedent, technical detail, and scholarship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review emphasizes that the two-level page distinguishes the fictitious pedagogical interaction from genuine historical practice; long footnotes that would elsewhere signal disorganization here enrich the reader by providing authoritative context and deeper material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for heuristic exposition over purely formalistic rigor in textbooks
rubrics_metrics.description: Favor the heuristic style of conjecture and refutation in mathematical treatises and textbooks rather than presenting mathematics only as once-tested, incontrovertible formal proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although Lakatos does not deny that full formalistic rigour is feasible, the review records his 'eloquent and conclusive case' for preferring heuristic exposition that reveals the discovery process, fallibility, and development of concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit testing of definitions via borderline and pathological examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions (e.g., what counts as a face of a polyhedron, planarity, connectedness) should be tested against borderline/pathological constructions to determine which stipulations are necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete borderline examples discussed include counting the faces of a star polyhedron as 12 versus 60, accepting a cylinder as a three-faced polyhedron, and other constructions that force rethinking of assumptions like planarity; these examples show the need to make assumptions explicit and justify them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of thought-experiments to decompose conjectures into testable subclaims
rubrics_metrics.description: Use hypothetical or thought-experimental proofs to break a conjecture into smaller subconjectures that can be individually examined and tested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review notes that tentative proofs often take the form of thought-experiments which expose the internal structure of a conjecture; this aids in locating the precise point of failure when counterexamples appear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention to historical scholarship and precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: Ground methodological claims and pedagogical examples in historical precedent and scholarship—show how historical mathematicians handled similar problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review highlights that the book's footnotes are nearly as voluminous as the text and provide historical precedents spanning three centuries; including such scholarship supports the methodological narrative and supplies authority and context.
